one_liner: Insertion-order-preserving hash map/set beating std::unordered_map on inserts, misses, and iteration.
what_it_does: Provides tsl::ordered_map and tsl::ordered_set, hash containers whose iteration order always matches insertion order, similar to Python's OrderedDict. Values are stored contiguously in a std::deque (default) or std::vector, directly exposed via values_container(); collisions are resolved with linear robin hood probing and backward shift deletion. The API mirrors std::unordered_map/std::unordered_set closely enough to be a near drop-in, adding heterogeneous lookup, precalculated-hash lookup, and serialize/deserialize helpers on top.
how_it_is_fast: Open addressing with linear robin hood probing plus backward shift deletion keeps probe sequences short and avoids tombstones, which speeds inserts and unsuccessful lookups relative to libstdc++'s node-based std::unordered_map. Storing values contiguously in a deque/vector instead of scattered nodes gives cache-friendly, pointer-chasing-free iteration, which is where the largest measured gains appear (22-45x). The tradeoff is an O(bucket_count) ordered erase() unless the O(1) pop_back()/unordered_erase() variants are used, which break insertion order.
when_to_use: Insert- and miss-heavy workloads on int64 or short/medium string keys, where 1.12-2.87x (inserts) and 2.34-4.40x (unsuccessful lookups) gains were measured
Need for insertion-order iteration (config/JSON-like objects, ordered dictionaries) that std::unordered_map cannot provide at all
Iteration-heavy code paths (serialization, dumping, full-container walks) - 22-45x faster than std::unordered_map in the cited shootout
Memory-constrained multi-million-entry containers (about 84MB vs 126MB at 3M int64 entries in the cited benchmark)
C++11-only toolchains that need a header-only, dependency-free drop-in with no build step
when_not_to_use: Erase-heavy workloads that must preserve order: erase() is O(bucket_count); only unordered_erase()/pop_back() are O(1) and they break ordering
Read-heavy workloads dominated by successful lookups: measured only 0.55-2.02x vs std::unordered_map, sometimes slower (e.g. read_random_shuffle_range)
Code relying on bucket-level APIs (bucket(), bucket_size(), ...): not supported

Decisions needing current-version confidence: the cited numbers are from v0.4 (2017) on an old i5-5200u laptop, not part of the newer Ankerl 2022 suite, and ordered_map is absent from the benchmark page's main charts
Containers needing more than 2^32-1 values without raising the IndexType template parameter

integration.dependencies: none (Boost Test only needed to build the test suite)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (tested with GCC 4.8.4, Clang 3.5.0, Visual Studio 2015); C++20 required only for the optional module build
integration.thread_safety: Same guarantee as std::unordered_map: multiple concurrent readers are safe, no concurrent writer
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: API closely mirrors std::unordered_map/set, but iterators are RandomAccessIterator, operator*/-> yield const std::pair<Key,T> (mutate via it.value(), not it->second), operator==/!= are order-dependent, and erase() is O(bucket_count) instead of O(1)

gotchas: erase() is O(bucket_count); use unordered_erase()/pop_back() for O(1) removal, but this breaks insertion order
Iterators expose const std::pair<Key,T>; modify values through it.value(), not it->second
operator==/!= are order-dependent: two containers with identical key/value pairs inserted in different order compare unequal
Default IndexType caps the container at 2,294,967,295 (2^32-1) values; raise the IndexType template parameter for larger sizes
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick tsl::ordered_map over the other cataloged std::unordered_map beaters (hopscotch_map, robin_map, ska flat/bytell, emhash, sparsepp, rigtorp/HashMap, libcuckoo, Verstable, dense_hash_map) when insertion-order iteration is a hard requirement - it is the only one of these that preserves order. Those siblings generally win on raw insert/lookup throughput but give no ordering guarantee at all.
verified_claims_summary: Author-run benchmark (Tessil hash-table-shootout, tsl::ordered_map v0.4) on an Intel i5-5200u/8GB RAM/Linux 4.11 with Clang 5.0 -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG, against libstdc++'s std::unordered_map: inserts 1.12-2.87x faster, unsuccessful lookups 2.34-4.40x faster, iteration 22-45x faster, successful lookups mixed at 0.55-2.02x, and about 84MB vs 126MB memory at 3M int64 entries.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-06-13, CI passing, MIT-licensed); header-only form makes it trivial to vendor and keep working even if upstream maintenance later lapses.
